mcqs.q: A dental composite is defined as:
opts: A 3-D combination of two or more chemically different materials with a distinct interface, superior to its components
mcqs.explain: A composite is a 3-dimensional combination of ≥2 chemically different materials with a distinct interface; the combination has superior properties.

mcqs.q: The acid-etching technique was introduced (1955) by:
mcqs.explain: M.G. Buonocore introduced the acid-etch technique in 1955; Bowen developed Bis-GMA resin in 1962.

mcqs.q: Bis-GMA (Bowen's resin) was developed in 1962 by:
mcqs.explain: Dr R.L. Bowen developed Bis-GMA (from bisphenol-A and glycidyl methacrylate) in 1962.

mcqs.q: The three MAJOR components of composite are:
opts: Resin matrix, inorganic fillers and coupling agents
mcqs.explain: The three major components are the resin matrix, inorganic fillers and coupling agents (plus minor components).

mcqs.q: The principal monomers of the resin matrix are:
mcqs.explain: The resin matrix is based on Bis-GMA (Bowen's resin) and UDMA; these are viscous, so a diluent monomer is added.

mcqs.q: A diluent monomer (e.g. TEGDMA) is added to the resin matrix to:
mcqs.explain: Bis-GMA/UDMA are highly viscous, so a diluent monomer is added to lower viscosity to a workable paste.

mcqs.q: Common inorganic fillers in composite include:
mcqs.explain: Inorganic fillers are quartz (early, poorly polishable), glass and silica.

mcqs.q: Which is a function of the inorganic fillers?
opts: Decrease wear, increase hardness, reduce shrinkage and add radiopacity
mcqs.explain: Fillers decrease wear, increase hardness, reduce polymerization shrinkage, increase radiopacity and contribute to esthetics.

mcqs.q: The coupling agent that bonds the filler to the resin matrix is:
mcqs.explain: Organosilanes are the most common coupling agents, promoting adhesion between the inorganic filler and the organic resin matrix.

mcqs.q: The photosensitizer (initiator) in light-cured composite is:
mcqs.explain: Camphorquinone is the photosensitizer, activated by visible blue light (400–500 nm).

mcqs.q: Composites are classified (Sturdevant) according to:
mcqs.explain: Sturdevant classifies composites by filler particle size: megafill, macrofill, midifill, minifill, microfill and nanofill.

mcqs.q: A MACROFILLED composite has a filler particle size of about:
mcqs.explain: Macrofilled composites have particles ~10–100 µm; they are strong but polish poorly.

mcqs.q: Microfilled composites are valued because they:
opts: Have very small particles and polish to a smooth surface
mcqs.explain: Microfilled composites (≈0.04 µm) have very small particles, giving a smooth, highly polishable surface (good for anteriors).

mcqs.q: HYBRID composites combine the advantages of:
mcqs.explain: Hybrids contain a mixture of particle sizes, giving good strength plus a polishable surface.

mcqs.q: Composite sets by which reaction?
mcqs.explain: Composite cures by free-radical polymerization (initiation, propagation, termination), which causes polymerization shrinkage.

mcqs.q: Light-cured composite is activated by:
mcqs.explain: Modern light-cured composites use camphorquinone activated by visible blue light (400–500 nm).

mcqs.q: Self-cured (chemically cured) composite is typically supplied as:
mcqs.explain: Self-cured composites come as two pastes that, when mixed, start the chemical free-radical polymerization.

mcqs.q: An inherent consequence of polymerization is:
mcqs.explain: Free-radical polymerization causes the composite to shrink (polymerization shrinkage), a key clinical concern.

mcqs.q: Minor components of composite include:
mcqs.explain: Minor components include initiators (camphorquinone), inhibitors (for shelf life) and pigments (for shade).

mcqs.q: Early quartz-filled composites had the drawback that they were:
mcqs.explain: Quartz (used in early composites) was hard to polish to a good surface, prompting the development of finer fillers.

mcqs.q: Adding more inorganic filler to a composite generally:
opts: Reduces polymerization shrinkage and improves wear resistance
mcqs.explain: Higher filler loading reduces polymerization shrinkage and improves hardness/wear resistance and radiopacity.

saqs.q: Define a composite and name its two historical advances.
saqs.a: A 3-D combination of two or more chemically different materials with a distinct interface. Advances: acid-etch (Buonocore 1955) and Bis-GMA resin (Bowen 1962).

saqs.q: List the three major components of composite.
saqs.a: Resin matrix (Bis-GMA/UDMA), inorganic fillers, and coupling agents (silane).

saqs.q: List the functions of the inorganic filler.
saqs.a: Decrease wear, increase hardness, reduce polymerization shrinkage, increase radiopacity, and improve esthetics.

saqs.q: What is the role of the coupling agent and an example?
saqs.a: Promotes adhesion between the filler and resin matrix; example: organosilane.

saqs.q: Classify composites by filler particle size.
saqs.a: Macrofill (10–100 µm), midifill, minifill, microfill (0.01–0.1 µm), nanofill, and hybrid (mixed).

saqs.q: Describe the activation methods of composite.
saqs.a: Self-cure (chemical, two pastes), light-cure (camphorquinone + blue light 400–500 nm), and dual-cure.
